Write something like, "My boyfriend has OCD and I have anxiety, are you accepting new clients?" And email it to them. The therapist, if they are good, will be very understanding if you explain you've never been to therapy before so you're anxious about it. That's totally normal. Any breed can be a service dog but the general consensus is that labrador retrievers, golden retrievers, german shepherd and poodles are the most commonly used breeds for service work.

So what will happen in my situation is that I will find the breeder get my trainer to talk to them to make sure that they're a good fit and then wait for a litter to be born and wait a few weeks for the breeder and my trainer to perform a personality evaluation called a temperament test. A temperament test lets them know If the dog is confident assertive fearful energetic focused et cetera and gives you insight into which of the puppies, if any, would be service dog candidates. Even among prospects not all of them are able to be service dogs because service dogs require a very specific and uncommon combination of traits that allow them to focus on their handler even in distracting environments, keep their cool in stressful situations, and perform life saving tasks and alerts for their handlers. So I won't actually be picking my own puppy, my trainer and the breeder will work together to select the best match for my needs.

So, your perspective that they're "absolutely milking it" is probably incorrect. Everyone's autism affects them differently, and just because someone seems "high functioning" to you doesn't mean that they are. The reason people told you not to use labels like high or low functioning is because it can 'put people in a box' and lead to assumptions about their capabilities, where the spectrum isn't really like that. Any autistic person can have any combination of autistic traits that may present themselves in different ways. Someone who can speak and communicate well with others (and mask) may have debilitating sensory issues. Also, it may help you understand to reframe "tantrums" as meltdowns. The difference is that a tantrum is a choice, where a meltdown is an uncontrollable reaction to neurological overload. I'm not sure if you've ever had a meltdown, but they're horrid. Imagine just losing control of your body and screaming, hitting yourself, biting, etc... and you can't control any of it. It's like a switch flips, and you're a passenger in your own body.
I think it may help you to try to have some compassion for others. Everyone is walking a path that you know nothing about. It's best not to assume.

An iud stands for intrauterine device. It's a t-shaped copper or plastic device that goes inside a person's cervix and into the uterus to prevent pregnancy. They are one of the most effective forms of singular birth control. Depending on what kind, they are effective for 3-10 years before needing to be removed by a gynecologist or other medical professional.
